Abstract 24

Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is implicated as a trigger of multiple sclerosis (MS), yet the host 25

genetic mechanisms linking EBV activity to MS is unknown. We performed a cross-ancestry 26

genome-wide association study of EBV DNA positivity (N=617,186), identifying 39 27

susceptibility risk loci that significantly overlapped with MS risk genes (p=1.3x10-12). Using 28

our single-cell method for EBV detection, we identified 1,069 EBV-infected B cells across 38 29

individuals. EBV was predominantly in the latent phase and B cell receptor analysis revealed 30

that memory B cell differentiation is altered by infection. Notably, EBV-infected switched 31

memory and atypical B cells upregulated cytokines and costimulatory signals that influence 32

T cell activation, and B cell signaling pathway. Finally, EBV-infected memory B cells 33

upregulated risk genes from both the EBV and MS, suggesting that EBV-infected B cells link 34

T cell modulation to activation of MS susceptibility pathways. These findings define a 35

genetically driven immunologic mechanism underlying MS. 36

Introduction 38

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the most frequent central nervous system (CNS) disease of 39

young adults. The disease most commonly begins with an autoimmune, relapsing remitting 40

phase mediated by circulating autoreactive T cells1 that migrate to the central nervous 41

system (CNS) and induce a marked inflammatory response both in the white matter and 42

cortical grey matter. A secondary, neurodegenerative disease course occurs in a significant 43

number of patients, presumably triggered by the initial T cell-mediated autoimmune process. 44

As with other autoimmune disorders, MS is triggered by environmental interactions in 45

genetically susceptible individuals. Indeed, we have identified 233 common genome loci 46

associated with disease risk and one variant associated with disease progression.2–4 The 47

majority of these map to the immune system, targeting T cells, regulatory T cells, and, in 48

particular, B cells.2,5,6 As a result, MS patients exhibit a spectrum of immunopathology, 49

including a skewing of T cells toward pro-inflammatory Th1 and Th17 programs,6–8 loss of 50

regulatory T-cell function with secretion of IFNγ,9,10 and activation of B cells.11 51

Compelling epidemiologic data implicates Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) as the initiating 52

event breaking immune tolerance in genetically susceptible individuals. A large longitudinal 53

study of U.S. military personnel reported that EBV infection occurs before MS 54

development12 , indicating that EBV is a necessary causal factor for MS. Serum 55

neurofilament light chain, a marker of axon injury, begins to rise only after EBV 56

seroconversion. Moreover, MS patients exhibit higher EBV activity,13–15 increased 57

frequencies of EBV-reactive T cells16,17, and EBV-derived antigens that cross-react with 58

myelin antigens 18–20. EBV primarily infects B cells, directly influencing their function21, and 59

we have observed distinctive alterations in B-cell phenotypes in MS (manuscript in 60

preparation). Importantly, B-cell depletion therapy is a highly effective treatment for the early 61

relapsing remitting, autoimmune phase of MS,22 underscoring the central role of B cells in 62

disease pathogenesis. 63

EBV plays a causal role in several other human diseases. Epidemiologic and 64

immunologic evidence links EBV to non-Hodgkin lymphoma, including Burkitt lymphoma, 65

nasopharyngeal carcinoma, gastric carcinoma, and, as discussed above, to MS, rheumatoid 66

arthritis (RA), and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).23 Although EBV infection is 67

ubiquitous, affecting more than 90% of the global population, its clinical manifestations vary 68

widely. In most individuals, EBV infection remains asymptomatic or latent, whereas a subset 69

of subjects develops infectious mononucleosis or chronic active EBV infection. Moreover, 70

infectious mononucleosis is not only a symptomatic form of EBV infection but also a strong 71

epidemiological risk factor for MS.24 However, few individuals develop malignancies or 72

autoimmune diseases after EBV infection. This variability suggests that the host’s ability to 73

EBV activity can be assessed through two major biomarkers: anti-EBV antibodies and 76

EBV DNA levels. Immunoglobulin (Ig) G targeting EBV antigens reflects prior exposure. 77

Over 90% of healthy adults and nearly 100% of patients with MS are seropositive.15,26 In 78

contrast, circulating EBV DNA provides a more direct readout of viral persistence, 79

reactivation burden, or reservoir dynamics; blood EBV DNA has been reported to be 80

elevated in patients with MS and SLE.14,27 Circulating EBV DNA is also clinically useful for 81

nasopharyngeal carcinoma screening.28 These complementary biomarkers therefore capture 82

distinct aspects of EBV biology and may reveal different dimensions of host genetic control. 83

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have enabled the identification of host 84

genetic variants influencing susceptibility to infection-related traits and pathogen burden. For 85

example, analysis of HIV viral load overcame the limited resolution of infection-status GWAS 86

and identified key loci in the HLA and CCR5 regions.29 Recent advances in sequencing 87

technologies now allow simultaneous quantification of host and viral genomes from the same 88

dataset. Our group previously developed VIRTUS,30 a pipeline for detecting viral transcripts 89

from RNA-seq data, and EBV detection from bulk RNA-seq has also been reported by 90

others.31 Similar WGS-based approaches have recently been applied to the human blood 91

virome, including a GWAS of human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) viral load that revealed 92

integration sites and links to SLE disease activity.32 For EBV, prior host-genetic studies have 93

largely focused on serologic antibody titers,33 which capture infection history rather than 94

DNA-based measures of viral activity. More recently, population-scale WGS studies have 95

demonstrated that EBV-derived reads can be quantified in large biobanks and that host 96

genetic determinants, particularly within the MHC, contribute to variation in EBV DNA 97

detection and persistence. These studies establish the feasibility of EBV DNA GWAS at a 98

biobank scale while motivating the need to define how these signals extend across ancestry 99

groups and connect to disease-relevant cellular phenotypes. 34–36 100

Here, we analyzed 617,186 participants from the All of Us Research Program37 and the 101

UK Biobank38 using harmonized viral-detection and quality-control pipelines across 102

ancestries and performed a cross-ancestry meta-analysis of EBV DNA positivity and viral 103

load. We extend this framework by jointly analyzing EBV DNA positivity and viral load, 104

integrating phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS), polygenic risk score (PRS) 105

analyses, Mendelian-randomization (MR)-based analyses, and HLA and ERAP2 106

interpretation to examine the shared host-genetic architecture linking EBV activity to human 107

disease (Fig. S1). Combining these population-scale analyses with single-cell RNA-seq 108

(scRNAseq) and spatial transcriptomic analyses, we identified specific cell types and 109

Together, these findings provide a multi-ancestry genetic and cellular framework for host 112

of EBV-infected B cells in people with MS, our study links population-scale EBV DNA signals 114

to disease-relevant cellular states and offers a mechanistic context for EBV-associated 115

Results 117 EBV DNA detection from WGS 118

To detect EBV reads in WGS datasets, we developed an analysis pipeline that filters 119

and counts reads mapped to the EBV decoy sequence in the human reference genome. We 120

applied our pipeline to the diverse cohort of study participants enrolled in the All of Us 121

Research Program. After quality control, 409,331 individuals were included. DNA information 122

was obtained from two sources: whole blood (N=359,796) and saliva (N=48,086). EBV DNA 123

was detected in 20.8% of blood samples and 52.7% of saliva samples. Age, sex, and 124

ancestry were significantly associated with EBV positivity. In both blood and saliva, higher 125

age was strongly associated with higher detection rates (Fig. 1A, blood: OR=1.16 per 10 126

years, 95% CI=1.15–1.16, p<1×10-100; saliva: OR=1.10 per 10 years, 95% CI=1.09–1.11, 127

p<1×10-65). Female sex was associated with a lower rate of EBV positivity compared with 128

males (Fig. 1A, blood: OR=0.83, 95% CI=0.81–0.84, p<1×10-100; saliva: OR=0.78, 95% 129

CI=0.75–0.81, p<1×10-35). 130

When examining ancestry, Europeans had the lowest EBV positivity, whereas all other 131

ancestries showed significantly higher odds ratios of EBV presence. In blood, African 132

(OR=2.17, p<1×10-100), Latino/admixed American (OR=2.02, p<1×10-100), East Asian 133

(OR=1.47, p=9.2×10⁻43), Middle Eastern (OR=1.31, p=1.2×10⁻4), and South Asians 134

(OR=1.29, p=6.1×10⁻11) ancestries had significantly higher odds ratios relative to Europeans 135

(Fig. S2A). In saliva, African (OR=1.61, p=4.1×10⁻65), Latino/admixed American (OR=2.02, 136

p<1×10-100), East Asian (OR=1.94, p=5.8×10⁻32) and South Asian ancestries also showed 137

increased odds (OR=1.42, p=1.4×10⁻5) (Fig. S2A). Middle Eastern ancestry showed a trend 138

for higher EBV positivity in saliva but did not reach statistical significance (OR=1.32, 139

p=0.078). 140

Next, we examined the distribution of EBV DNA load. When normalized by the number 141

of reads mapped to the human genome, the EBV DNA load was on average 3,826-fold 142

higher in saliva compared to blood (Fig. 1B). Moreover, a subset of individuals carried viral 143

loads that far exceeded the population average. Indeed, in blood, the top 1% of samples 144

accounted for 64% of the total EBV DNA load, with the top 5% and 10% contributing 83% 145

These findings demonstrate that the distribution of EBV DNA load is heavy-tailed in both 153

To comprehensively investigate diseases co-occurring with EBV infection, we 156

conducted a Phenome-wide Association Study (PheWAS). Using European-ancestry 157

participants from All of Us, we performed a PheWAS of EBV DNA positivity and viral load 158

(Figs. S2B, C, Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). As recently reported,35 we confirmed that 159

both EBV DNA positivity and viral load showed strong associations with immunosuppressive 160

conditions such as HIV infection and post-transplant immunosuppression, as well as with 161

tobacco use and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).39 Furthermore, the 162

analysis identified a significant association with infectious mononucleosis, a manifestation of 163

primary EBV infection in adolescents. Unexpectedly, neither MS nor SLE emerged as 164

positively associated traits (MS: EBV positivity, OR=0.83, FDR=0.034; viral load, FDR=0.78. 165

SLE: EBV positivity, FDR=0.27; viral load, FDR=0.96). In addition to confirming known 166

associations with rheumatoid arthritis, we observed correlations with encephalitis, 167

encephalopathy, and polyneuropathies, suggesting links to other inflammatory neurological 168

diseases. Although more traits were significantly associated with EBV DNA positivity 169

(FDR<0.05, 475 traits) than with EBV viral load (270 traits), the viral load analysis 170

specifically highlighted associations with virus-related malignancies such as non-Hodgkin 171

lymphoma and T cell lymphoma, as well as myopathy. The PheWAS results not only 172

reproduced well-established associations between EBV and related diseases, validating our 173

analytical pipeline, but also revealed broader links to autoimmune and inflammatory 174

disorders, underscoring the extensive disease spectrum influenced by EBV infection. 175

Multi-Ancestry genome-wide association study of EBV DNA 176

blood-derived samples from the All of Us cohort. We selected 5,020,877 SNPs with a minor 180

allele frequency (MAF) of ≥1% in All of Us (Methods). Association tests were performed 181

Next, we examined the lead SNPs within each locus in detail. Outside of the HLA region, 200

approximately half of the associated variants were intronic (Supplementary Table 4, 201

positivity: 63.1%; viral load: 53.3%), and roughly half were located in cis-eQTLs 202

(Supplementary Table 4, positivity :55%; viral load: 60%). The majority of these loci 203

(Supplementary Table 4, positivity: 65.8%; viral load: 60%) have been previously implicated 204

in immune-related traits, including MS, SLE, RA, IgM levels, and blood cell counts in prior 205

GWAS (Fig. 1C). Remarkably, there was a significant overlap with genetic variants 206

associated with MS risk (Fig. 1D, OR=32.1, p=1.3x10-12) and severity (Fig. 1D, OR=180.6, 207

p=7.54x10-3) including MS susceptibility alleles, HLA-DRB1*04:04, HLA-A*02:01 and to a 208

lesser extent, HLA-DRB1*15:01. Specifically, among the top hits, 29.7% of the EBV 209

positivity-associated genes and 33% of the viral load-associated genes overlapped with 210

genes reported in our MS GWAS, including DYSF, which has been associated with MS 211

severity4 (Figs. 1C and S4A). When we examined the direction of effects for EBV DNA 212

positivity across autoimmune diseases, we found that a number genetic variants, including 213

SLAMF7, CTLA4, EOMES, CD86, TP63, TRAF3, CLEC16A, RSBN1, and IKZF3 showed 214

concordant effects, with increased EBV DNA positivity associated with increased disease 215

risk, while SP140, SH2B3, and PTPN11 exhibited discordant directions of effect with less 216

EBV DNA presence (Fig. 1C). The genes highlighted by the GWAS provided biological 217

insights into the regulation of EBV activity. For example, TERT, encoding the catalytic 218

Stratified LD score regression49 revealed that genetic heritability for both EBV DNA 227

positivity and EBV DNA load was concentrated in transcriptionally active genomic regions, 228

particularly at transcription start sites (TSS; enrichment=23.4±4.1 [positivity], 31.3±5.3 [load]), 229

FANTOM5 enhancers (19.9±10.3 [positivity], 32.7±13.8 [load]), and coding regions (17.2±5.2 230

Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that EBV susceptibility loci were primarily 233

concentrated in immune response–related pathways (Fig. S4E, Supplementary Tables 7 and 234

8). Both EBV positivity and EBV DNA load showed significant enrichment for T cell activation, 235

CD8+ αβ T cell activation, and T cell proliferation, reflecting a shared involvement of 236

cytotoxic T cell–mediated immune responses. Cell cycle G1/S phase transition was 237

specifically enriched for EBV positivity, while EBV DNA load additionally involved epithelial- 238

associated pathways such as positive regulation of keratinocyte proliferation and 239

multiciliated epithelial cell differentiation, indicating potential contributions of epithelial cell 240

proliferation and differentiation to viral load regulation. 241

To assess the effects of GWAS-prioritized host genes on EBV transcriptional activity, 242

we performed siRNA-mediated knockdown of candidate genes and analyzed EBV 243

transcripts (Fig. 1F). Knockdown of EBV DNA GWAS-prioritized host genes altered EBV 244

transcriptional activity and, at 72 hours, was associated with a shift toward reduced EBV 245

gene expression (Figs. 1G and S6). This was more pronounced for lytic-associated 246

transcripts than for latent-associated transcripts. Consistent with this pattern, for example, 247

SP140 knockdown reduced BLLF1 expression, whereas PARP15 knockdown decreased 248

LMP2 and BMRF1. However, these effects were not uniform, including a transient increase 249

in latent transcripts after IKZF3 knockdown and increased EBNA2 expression at 72 hours 250

after PARP15 knockdown. Together, these findings suggest that EBV DNA GWAS hit genes 251

contribute to the regulation of EBV transcription, but their effects are not simply binary; rather, 252

they act in a transcript-selective and time-dependent manner, with a broader repressive 253

trend emerging at later time points. 254

To further test the causal relationship between EBV and autoimmune diseases, we 255

performed bidirectional Mendelian randomization using 27 independent SNPs associated 256

with EBV DNA positivity (Fig. S5A, Supplementary Tables 9). Genetically predicted EBV 257

DNA positivity was associated with increased risk of MS (OR=1.45, 95% CI=1.18–1.80), RA 258

(OR=1.27, 95% CI=1.05–1.54), and SLE (OR=1.44, 95% CI=1.08–1.91), but not ischemic 259

stroke, used as a negative control. These effects were predominantly driven by MHC 260

variants, and reverse MR analyses did not support an effect of autoimmune disease liability 261

on EBV DNA levels. Together, these results support a unidirectional contribution of 262

genetically determined EBV activity to autoimmune disease risk, largely mediated by MHC 263

variation. 264

To investigate whether the polygenic architecture of EBV activity contributes to 265

autoimmune disease risk, we constructed PRSs from the EBV DNA GWAS in the European 266

ancestry subset of the All of Us cohort and tested them in European ancestry participants in 267

the UK Biobank (N=487,181; 2,423 MS cases; Fig. S5B, Supplementary Tables 10). A one– 268

standard deviation increase in the EBV DNA positivity PRS was associated with increased 269

risk of MS (OR=1.11, 95% CI=1.07–1.16, p<0.0001), with individuals in the top PRS decile 270

showing higher MS prevalence than those in the bottom decile (0.68% vs 0.52%; OR=1.33, 271

95% CI=1.13–1.57). Partitioning the PRS revealed that this association was largely driven by 272

variants within the MHC region, whereas non-MHC variants showed no significant effect. 273

Together, these results indicate that host genetic variation shapes EBV activity, with a 274

substantial contribution from immune regulatory loci and the MHC region, linking genetically 275

determined EBV control to autoimmune disease susceptibility. 276

Polygenic risk scoring and EBV DNA measured by quantitative PCR (qPCR) 277

To evaluate whether identified genome-wide significant risk loci for EBV DNA capture 278

biologically meaningful variation in viral load, we assessed PRSs in an independent cohort 279

with qPCR-based measurement of EBV DNA. We calculated PRSs based on risk variants 280

identified in the meta-analysis of European ancestry using PRScs.50 We evaluated 281

association with EBV DNA positivity measured by qPCR in an independent Yale cohort of 282

European ancestry (Fig. 1E, S5C, and Supplementary Tables 11; N=94; mean age 283

40.2±14.7 years; 71% female). EBV DNA positivity was 2/10 (20%) in the top decile, 1/74 284

(1.4%) in the middle group, and 0/10 (0%) in the bottom decile for both positivity and viral 285

load PRS (Ordinal trend tests positivity: p=0.024; viral load: p=0.016). Consistently, one 286

standard deviation increase in the PRS was associated with a higher EBV DNA load after 287

adjustment (log10 EBNA1 copies/mL) (positivity: β=0.21, SE=0.076, p=0.006; load: β=0.26, 288

SE=0.075, p=0.0009). When we stratified variants by their location inside or outside the 289

MHC region, only the PRSs derived from the MHC region showed significant associations 290

Antigen presentation by HLA and EBV activity 296

The strongest associations in both GWASs were located within the HLA locus. In 297

addition, a secondary genome-wide significant signal was identified at rs27300, a variant 298

residing within a linkage disequilibrium block encompassing the LNPEP and ERAP1/2 genes 299

(Figs. 2A and S6A). This variant exhibited a significant eQTL effect on ERAP2 expression in 300

lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) (p=2.33x10-118, Fig. 2B), but not with LNPEP (p=7.07x10-6, 301

*Fig. 2B). ERAP2 encodes an aminopeptidase essential for peptide trimming selectively 302*

during antigen presentation via MHC class I molecules. This allelic directionality provides 303

additional support for a functional role of ERAP2 in EBV control. The ERAP2-increasing C 304

allele corresponds to the protective direction in the EBV GWAS, suggesting that more 305

efficient peptide trimming enhances antigen presentation and improves the clearance of 306

EBV-infected cells. 307

We also investigated the associations with HLA alleles and amino acid usage and EBV 308

susceptibility. Using All of Us participants of European ancestry, classical HLA alleles were 309

imputed with SNP2HLA,51 and their associations with EBV activity (DNA positivity and DNA 310

viral load) were examined. In both traits, HLA-DRB1*04:04 showed the most significant 311

association. After conditioning analysis, the top alleles associated with EBV DNA positivity 312

were HLA-DRB1*04:04, B*14:02, A*02:01, DQA1*05, and B*35:01, while those for EBV DNA 313

load were HLA-DRB1*04:04, A*02:01, B*35:01, DQA1*05:01, and B*14, showing a broadly 314

consistent pattern between the two traits (Fig. 2C and S6B, 7, 8, Supplementary Tables 12, 315

13). While to a lesser degree, EBV DNA positivity was also seen with the strongest MHC 316

associated allele, DRB1*15:01. Furthermore, an amino acid–level association analysis 317

identified multiple residues significantly correlated with EBV activity (Figs. 2C, S6B, S7, S8, 318

and Supplementary Tables 14, 15). Notably, valine at position 95 of HLA-A*02:01 (A95V), 319

detected in both positivity and viral load analyses, was located within the F pocket of the 320

peptide-binding groove, while position 30 of HLA-DRB1 (L/R/Y variants), detected in the viral 321

load analysis, was located in the P7 pocket (Fig. 2D). Both residues are situated within key 322

structural regions that determine peptide-binding specificity, suggesting that EBV-associated 323

HLA signals may reflect functional variation in peptide-binding pockets influencing viral 324

antigen presentation and immune recognition. 325

mucosal immune environments contribute to host susceptibility to EBV activity. In contrast, 342

by spleen, lymphoid tissue, and blood, indicating a link between viral load regulation and B 344

Discussion 495

Here, we developed a pipeline to quantify EBV DNA from whole-genome sequencing 496

data and applied it to population-scale cohorts. A cross-ancestry GWAS of EBV DNA 497

positivity in 617,186 individuals identified 39 susceptibility risk loci. We validated this finding 498

in our independent cohort and found that qPCR-confirmed EBV DNA-positive individuals 499

were markedly enriched in the top decile of EBV polygenic risk scores containing these 500

newly discovered loci. Intriguingly, there was a significant overlap with genetic variants 501

associated with MS, RA, and SLE susceptibility alleles, and Mendelian randomization 502

analyses further supported a causal influence of EBV activity on MS, largely driven by HLA 503

variation. By establishing a single-cell RNA-seq method optimized for EBER1 detection, we 504

found that EBV RNA was detected primarily in memory, atypical, and antibody-secreting B 505

MS is the autoimmune disease for which EBV is most strongly implicated as a 515

Moreover, it has been clearly demonstrated that the EBV virus harbors sequences that are 518

Although EBV DNA showed no positive association with MS in our PheWAS,63 a well- 523

controlled treatment-naive MS cohort and the case-control meta-analyses showed elevated 524

EBV DNA levels in MS patients. This discrepancy is likely explained by the time course of 525

EBV involvement in the onset of MS. Specifically, EBV seroconversion occurs an average of 526

7.5 years before clinical onset,12 MS diagnosis requires CNS lesions disseminated in time 527

and space,64 and a prodromal period precedes diagnosis.65 As a result, EBV load at the time 528

of diagnosis is likely to be partially deflated. Furthermore, individuals with MS in cohorts such 529

as All of Us include patients receiving long-term immunotherapy and those many years after 530

diagnosis, making it difficult to capture EBV activity during the true initiation phase. These 531

considerations highlight the importance of examining newly diagnosed, treatment-naïve 532

patients or MS high-risk individuals prior to disease onset to accurately evaluate EBV activity 533

in early MS. 534

Recent population-scale studies established the feasibility of quantifying EBV DNA from 535

WGS data and highlighted genetic factors for controlling EBV persistence.35,36 However, the 536

relationship between EBV activity and MS appears to depend on the level of genetic 537

modest, consistent with our own observations that diffuse genome-wide correlation is 539

limited.36 By contrast, when focusing on lead EBV-associated loci, we observed clear 540

overlap with established MS susceptibility loci. One plausible explanation is that the 541

EBV DNA quantification from WGS 711

The human reference genome, GRCh38, which is used in AoU and UKB, contains the EBV 712

decoy sequence, named chrEBV. To detect EBV reads in WGS samples, we investigated 713

reads mapped to chrEBV stored in the CRAM files. A WGS sample can sometimes contain 714

very abundant EBV reads due to viremia and have the potential to cause a heavy 715

computational burden. To decrease the computational cost, samples with more than 350,000 716

reads mapped to chrEBV were randomly downsampled using samtools to 350,000 reads. 717

Reads were then filtered to retain only proper pairs, passing standard quality control metrics, 718

with duplicates, secondary, and supplementary alignments removed. Mapping length was 719

repetitive nature of the BamHI W repeat region in the EBV reference genome. Our pipeline 723

accounts for this repetitive nature and avoids counting such multi-mapping reads repeatedly. 724

summarized separately inside and outside the BamHI W repeat. In the case of analysis with 726
